items.answer: Expert evaluation is a quick, cheap usability test of a prototype at an early design stage, in which design-team members or domain experts independently report usability issues, and a few end users may be included optionally.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.

Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.

The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) is a widely used questionnaire for measuring cybersickness in immersive experiences. It contains 16 items in oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales, rated from 0 to 3, with subscale and total sickness scores.

questions.question: What distinguishes user evaluation from expert evaluation?
options: It asks users directly, so user participation is required
It asks experts directly, so user participation is optional
It asks users directly, so expert participation is required
It asks users indirectly, so user participation is optional
questions.explanation: User evaluation obtains feedback by asking users directly, so it requires user involvement. Expert evaluation does not have the same requirement for user participation.

questions.question: What can the items in a user-evaluation self-report instrument take the form of?
options: Questions or tasks for users to perform
Questions or statements for users to rate
Statements or ratings for experts to judge
Tasks or errors for observers to score
questions.explanation: In user evaluation, feedback is collected with rating scales, and the items provided for rating can be questions or statements. They are not tasks, errors, or expert judgment items.

questions.question: Why are post-task and post-session questionnaires not necessarily the same in user evaluation?
options: The items need to match the point at which feedback is collected
The items need to describe every task at the end of the session
The items need to be identical at every collection point
The items need to describe the whole session after each task
questions.explanation: Feedback can be collected after each task and after the whole session, and the questionnaire should be suited to the point of collection. Therefore the post-task and post-session instruments may differ.

data.text: User evaluation is a self-report technique that asks users directly to answer rating scales, producing subjective or preference data and making feedback easier to collect than with more rigorous methods. The rating items are questions or statements, commonly called questionnaires, and suitable questionnaires are challenging to identify. Feedback can be collected after each task, after the session, or both when feasible, with questionnaires matched to the point; standard post-task instruments include ASQ and EM, while standard post-session instruments include SUS, CSUQ, QUIS, and USE.
points: User evaluation is a self-report technique requiring users to directly answer rating scales, yielding subjective or preference data.
Collecting rating-scale feedback in user evaluation is easier than more rigorous evaluation techniques.
User-evaluation questionnaires are questions or statements for users to rate, and choosing suitable ones is challenging.
User feedback may be collected after each task, after the session, or both if feasible, with matching questionnaires.
Well-known post-task questionnaires include ASQ and EM; well-known post-session questionnaires include SUS, CSUQ, QUIS, and USE.

questions.question: The After Scenario Questionnaire is a questionnaire administered when?
options: before users have started the tasks in a scenario
after users have completed the whole evaluation session
while users are still completing the tasks in a scenario
after users have completed the tasks in a scenario
questions.explanation: The ASQ is described as a post-task questionnaire, so it follows completion of the tasks rather than the whole session or an in-progress task.

questions.question: In the ISO usability mapping for the After Scenario Questionnaire, which measure is linked to the amount of time taken to complete tasks?
options: Efficiency
Satisfaction
Effectiveness
Learnability
questions.explanation: Time taken maps to efficiency, while ease maps to effectiveness; the three statements together represent satisfaction.

questions.question: How can the feedback collected with the After Scenario Questionnaire be summarised?
options: Averaging the ease ratings or averaging the time ratings
Averaging each statement's ratings or averaging all statements' ratings
Averaging each user's ratings or averaging all users' ratings
Averaging the post-task ratings or averaging the post-session ratings
questions.explanation: ASQ feedback can be summarised by averaging ratings for each statement across users or by averaging ratings across all statements; the other options mix in per-user or post-session summaries that are not the described method.

data.text: The After Scenario Questionnaire is a post-task instrument that captures how satisfied users are with task ease, task time, and support information. By rating those three statements on a seven-point agreement scale, the questionnaire produces usability feedback that aligns with ISO measures: ease as effectiveness, time as efficiency, and the combined statements as satisfaction. Those ratings can then be reduced to averages either for each statement across users or for all statements together.
points: The After Scenario Questionnaire is a post-task questionnaire with three statements about task ease, task time, and support information.
In the After Scenario Questionnaire, users rate each statement from 1, strongly disagree, to 7, strongly agree.
Per ISO usability, the After Scenario Questionnaire roughly maps ease to effectiveness, time to efficiency, and statements together to satisfaction.
The After Scenario Questionnaire can be summarised by averaging each statement across users or all statements together.

questions.question: How are users asked to respond to each item in the System Usability Scale?
options: by rating satisfaction with a statement
by rating agreement with a statement
by reporting a specific difficulty in their own words
by rating agreement with a question
questions.explanation: SUS items are statements, not questions, and users rate how strongly they agree with each statement.

questions.question: Why does the System Usability Scale calculation treat even-numbered item ratings differently from odd-numbered item ratings?
options: Because the even-numbered items are negatively worded counterparts of the preceding odd items
Because the even-numbered items describe separate tasks rather than the whole system
Because the even-numbered items are rated on a seven-point scale
Because the even-numbered items are completed by expert evaluators rather than users
questions.explanation: The formula reverses even-numbered ratings because those statements are negatively worded counterparts of the preceding odd-numbered statements.

questions.question: What does a System Usability Scale score of 70 or higher typically indicate?
options: An interface that produced a detailed report from each evaluator
An interface that was rated on a seven-point scale
An interface that already explains the causes of its problems
A usable interface with only minimal problems
questions.explanation: A score of 70 or higher is treated as desirable because it suggests the interface is usable or has only minimal problems.

questions.question: Compared with expert evaluation techniques, what does the System Usability Scale give designers?
options: A quick general indication that usability problems may exist
A list of the exact causes behind every usability problem
A detailed report from each evaluator about specific violations
A replacement for further brainstorming or examination of statement scores
questions.explanation: SUS gives a quick overall signal about usability problems, but it does not explain their reasons, so designers must look further.

data.text: The System Usability Scale evaluates a system after a completed session by asking users to rate ten short statements. The statements alternate in wording, and their 5-point ratings are combined by a fixed formula into a single score. That score is interpreted as a percentage, with 70% or higher typically indicating a usable system and lower scores suggesting problems. SUS provides a quick user-based signal of usability problems, but it does not explain the causes, so designers must investigate the issues separately.
points: The System Usability Scale is a post-session questionnaire using statements rather than questions after all tasks.
The System Usability Scale has ten statements, with each even-numbered statement as the negative counterpart of the preceding odd statement.
System Usability Scale ratings are 1–5; score = 2.5 × (sum odd rating−1 plus sum 5−even rating).
System Usability Scale scores are read as percentages; 70% or higher is typically desirable, below may need design review.
Unlike expert evaluation, System Usability Scale ratings quickly signal usability problems but not reasons, so designers must identify specific problems.

questions.question: Which property makes ASQ and SUS less targeted than tools built for XR sickness?
options: They measure susceptibility to motion sickness
They assess nausea in immersive displays
They are generic to any interactive system
They target overall discomfort in immersive sessions
questions.explanation: ASQ and SUS are general instruments for interactive systems, so they do not specifically address XR sickness, nausea, or susceptibility.

questions.question: How is the simulator sickness questionnaire positioned among instruments for assessing sickness?
options: It is the susceptibility instrument for motion sickness
It is the generic instrument for interactive systems
It is the short instrument for specific motion states
It is the most used instrument for XR sickness
questions.explanation: The simulator sickness questionnaire is the most extensively used instrument specifically designed for sickness in XR, not a generic, short, or susceptibility instrument.

questions.question: For which experience type is the cyber sickness questionnaire considered good?
options: VR experiences with standard monitors
AR experiences with see-through displays
MR experiences with passthrough cameras
VR experiences with head-mounted displays
questions.explanation: The cyber sickness questionnaire is good for VR experiences with head-mounted displays, not for AR see-through, MR passthrough, or standard-monitor setups.

questions.question: What is the distinguishing feature of the misery scale and the fast motion sickness scale?
options: They are generic usability measures for any system
They are scales for overall immersive discomfort
They are susceptibility measures for motion sickness
They are shorter, more precise, and more concise
questions.explanation: MIS and FMS are shorter, more precise, and more concise XR questionnaires for specific conditions, not generic, susceptibility, or general discomfort scales.

data.text: Questionnaires for general interactive systems are separated from questionnaires designed for XR discomfort. The XR-specific instruments are organized around what they assess: cybersickness, specific conditions, susceptibility to cyber sickness, and overall discomfort. This arrangement makes it clearer which questionnaire matches which XR evaluation target.
points: ASQ and SUS are generic questionnaires for interactive systems, not specifically for XR.
SSQ, VRSQ, and CSQ address XR cybersickness; SSQ is most extensively used and CSQ fits HMD VR.
MIS and FMS are shorter, more precise, more concise questionnaires assessing specific XR conditions.
MHQ, MSSQ, and VIMSSQ measure susceptibility to cyber sickness in XR.
The nausea scale and MSAQ commonly assess overall discomfort in immersive XR experiences.

questions.question: What role did real images play in creating the 3D models for the Majuli VR Tour?
options: They were compressed to reduce the mobile application size
They were loaded from cloud storage when a thumbnail was clicked
They replaced the 3D modeling process in Autodesk Maya
They provided references and textures for the modeled objects
questions.explanation: Real images were used as references and textures while the 3D models were created, not as a substitute for modeling or as streamed or compressed media.

questions.question: What change reduced the Oculus Quest Majuli VR Tour from 9.85 GB to 5.1 GB?
options: Compression of high-resolution 360-degree and 2D images for mobile deployment
Removal of most video playback support from the headset build
Replacement of the 3D models by a smaller set of 360-degree images
Cloud storage of all videos, with loading after a thumbnail click
questions.explanation: The Quest version was made smaller by moving videos to cloud storage and loading them on demand after a thumbnail click; the other options describe mobile-version reductions or unsupported changes.

questions.question: What change made the Google Cardboard Majuli VR Tour small enough for mobile deployment?
options: Compressing 360-degree and 2D images and removing most video playback support
Lowering the Android version requirement and removing the headset toolkit from the mobile build
Compressing the cultural videos and leaving the drone videos in the mobile build
Replacing the 3D models with 360-degree images and reducing the audio files for mobile deployment
questions.explanation: The mobile version was reduced by compressing 360-degree and 2D images and removing most video playback support. Lowering the Android requirement or swapping other media content does not match the mobile size reduction.

data.text: The Majuli VR Tour was implemented in Unity for Oculus Quest 2 and Android, using the XR toolkit for Quest and the Google VR SDK for Cardboard, with 3D models created in Autodesk Maya. Its full geographic content made the initial package 9.85 GB, so the Quest version loaded clicked videos from the cloud and reduced the app to 5.1 GB. The Google Cardboard version was smaller at 0.7 GB because it compressed images and removed most video playback, keeping one initial 360-degree video.
points: The Majuli VR Tour used Unity 2021.3.22f1 for Oculus Quest 2 and Android smartphones requiring Android 6.0.
The Majuli VR Tour used the XR toolkit for Oculus Quest and the Google VR SDK for Google Cardboard.
Autodesk Maya created the Majuli VR Tour’s 3D models using real images as references and textures.
Loading clicked Oculus Quest videos from the cloud reduced the Majuli VR Tour from 9.85 GB to 5.1 GB.
Compressing images and removing most video support made the Google Cardboard Majuli VR Tour 0.7 GB.

activities.title: Order the size-optimization steps of the Majuli VR Tour

items.title: Order the size-optimization steps of the Majuli VR Tour
steps: The application is built from content that covers the entire geographic spread
Videos are stored in cloud services and loaded from thumbnails when clicked
A mobile Google Cardboard version is made by compressing images and removing most video playback support

questions.question: What makes the model-based Majuli VR Tour appear realistic without using 360-degree image captures?
options: Its 3D models are textured with real images
Its boat-ride footage is captured from field trips
Its 360-degree photos are compressed for mobile
Its cultural videos are stored in cloud services
questions.explanation: The model-based tour builds the experience from 3D models and gives them a realistic look by applying textures taken from real images. Compression, boat-ride footage, and cloud video storage belong to other parts or versions of the tour.

questions.question: In the 360-degree-image Majuli VR Tour, what does the user experience immediately after group selection?
options: Arrow-key movement inside a location
A tablet interface for selecting a map location
A boat ride from the mainland to the island
A notification for an available cultural video
questions.explanation: Immediately after group selection, the user takes a boat ride from the mainland to Majuli island, using 360-degree video captured during field trips. The tablet interface, arrow-key movement, and cultural-video notifications occur at later points in the experience.

questions.question: When the user reaches the riverbank in the 360-degree-image Majuli VR Tour, what does the tablet interface let the user do?
options: Press arrow keys and move forward or back
Select a map location and move there
Watch an introductory video and learn controls
Open a cultural video and receive a notice
questions.explanation: At the riverbank, a tablet interface appears so the user can choose a place on a map and move there. The tutorial, cultural-video notification, and arrow-key movement belong to other parts of the 360-degree-image tour.

questions.question: In the 360-degree-image Majuli VR Tour, how is movement from one point to another presented to the user?
options: A drone flythrough with manual teleportation
A free walking path with manual teleportation
A boat ride path with manual teleportation
A fixed vehicle route with teleportation
questions.explanation: Travel between points uses teleportation combined with a fixed road route, so the user feels motion as if riding a vehicle along the road. The boat ride is the arrival sequence, not the point-to-point travel method.

questions.question: What does the Google Cardboard Majuli VR Tour retain from the full Oculus Quest experience?
options: Campus models and village models
Ambient sound and a full video set
Cultural videos and a video player
A boat ride and a minimap
questions.explanation: The mobile Google Cardboard version is reduced in size and features, but it keeps the boat-ride experience and a tablet-like interface with a minimap. It omits most videos and does not use the 3D-model tour's campus models.

data.text: Three Majuli VR Tour implementations adapt the tour to different hardware. The Oculus Quest 360-degree-image tour uses media and a guided flow: introduction, boat ride, tablet map, local movement, and fixed-route teleportation between 360-degree views. The 3D-model Quest tour replaces that media-based approach with textured models of the island, while the smartphone-based Google Cardboard version reduces features and videos but keeps the main navigation, boat ride, and minimap.
points: The Majuli VR Tour has three implementations: 360-degree-image and 3D-model Oculus Quest tours and a Google Cardboard mobile tour.
The 360-degree-image Quest tour uses images, videos, sound, ray-cast selection, a boat ride and tablet map selection.
Inside 360-degree locations, users move with arrow keys, see icons and cultural videos, and travel via minimap vehicle-metaphor teleportation.
The 3D-model Quest tour replaces images or videos with textured models of Kamalabadi Satra, campus roads, villages and dwellings.
The smartphone-based Google Cardboard tour is a reduced Quest version: fewer videos, but similar controls, boat ride and minimaps.

questions.question: How did the heavy content of the Majuli virtual reality system shape the size-reduction strategy used for its Oculus Quest and Google Cardboard versions?
questions.reference_answer: The initial system was 9.85 GB because its content covered the entire geographic spread. Moving videos to the cloud and loading them on demand reduced the client application to 5.1 GB. Because that size was not suitable for mobile deployment, the Google Cardboard version compressed high-resolution 360-degree and 2D images and removed most video playback, reaching 0.7 GB.

questions.question: Why can the After Scenario Questionnaire and the System Usability Scale both be used in user evaluation, even though they are administered at different stages?
questions.reference_answer: User evaluation can collect feedback after each task and at the end of a session, and using both points is desirable if feasible. The After Scenario Questionnaire is a post-task questionnaire whose statements relate to effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction. The System Usability Scale is a post-session questionnaire that gives a quick general indication of whether usability problems exist after all tasks are completed.

questions.question: Why is the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire a suitable complement to generic usability questionnaires for evaluating the Majuli virtual reality tour?
questions.reference_answer: The After Scenario Questionnaire and System Usability Scale are generic questionnaires applicable to any interactive system, not specifically meant for extended reality. The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire is the most extensively used questionnaire specifically designed for cybersickness in extended reality. Cybersickness is primarily relevant to virtual reality, so it addresses a problem that generic usability questionnaires do not specifically target.

questions.question: How does the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality tour use teleportation to support travel between locations?
questions.reference_answer: It uses teleportation, a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user points to a desired virtual location and is sent there without physical movement. In this tour, travel from one point to another combines that instant change of viewpoint with a vehicle-metaphor route-planning method. The road route is fixed, and the user experiences motion as if riding a vehicle along the road.
